> 吾生也有涯，而知也無涯。以有涯隨無涯，殆已。

Life has a limit; knowledge does not. To chase the unlimited with the limited — 殆, exhausted, and that is the end of it.

The chapter that follows contains the most famous knife in Chinese philosophy. It is usually read as a lesson in skill: practice until you can carve a ox without blunting the blade. The book reads it as a lesson in where to put the blade.

## 涯 is a shoreline

涯: water with a bank. 有涯 is not "short." It is "bounded" — a life has an edge, the way a shore has one.

無涯 is the other side: knowledge, judgments, reputations, projects, each without a shore.

The sentence is not an anti-intellectual slogan. It is a ratio: a bounded thing is being spent on an unbounded thing, and the spending is what 殆 describes.

## 督 means the middle

緣督以為經 — take the middle as the constant.

Here a note is needed. Reading 督 as "the governing vessel" (督脈) comes from 成玄英's subcommentary; reading it as 中 comes from 李頤's gloss, 督，中也. The two point at the same place — the central channel is the middle way — but the book takes 中 as the base sense and 督脈 as the explanatory one, without ranking them.

中 here is not compromise. It is the empty, unbiased passage — 守中, not splitting the difference.

## 郤 is a gap, and the gap was already there

郤 (隙): a gap, a seam. 天理 in this chapter is not "the laws of nature." It is the grain of a thing — the seams it already has.

游刃: the blade moves in the gap. The gap was not made by the blade. That is the whole of the skill, and it is not a technique — it is an observation.

## 肯綮 is where things knot

肯: flesh attached to bone. 綮: the place where tendon and bone cross and bind — the knotted, blocked, hardest passage. The image for any entanglement that will not come apart by force.

The line 技經肯綮之未嘗 (one edition: 枝經) means: the blade never even touched the places where tendons cross — how much less the big bones.

## 縣解: the suspension lets go

縣 is to hang, to be suspended; 解 is to untie. 帝之縣解 — the untying that comes from 帝.

But 帝 here is not a god. 郭象: 帝者，天之名也 — 帝 is a name for the natural. What hangs you is natural too: grief and joy, tied to gain and loss. 縣解 is that knot loosening by itself.

## 薪 and 火

薪: firewood, the body. 火: the flame, the awareness that does not depend on one piece of wood.

The line is often quoted at funerals. Its argument is narrower and stronger: what burns is consumed; what is passed on is not the same thing as what burned.

## The test

Where is your blade hitting bone? Name one recurring difficulty — a person, a task, a conversation — and locate the 肯綮: the exact knot, not the general area. If you cannot name the seam, you are cutting by force, and the blade is wearing.
